In [[functional analysis]], the '''Shilov boundary''' is the smallest   [[closed set|closed]] subset of the [[structure space]] of a [[commutative]] [[Banach algebra]] where an analog of the [[maximum modulus principle]] holds. It is named after its discoverer, [[Georgii Evgen'evich Shilov]].

== Precise definition and existence ==
Let <math>\mathcal A</math> be a [[commutative]] [[Banach algebra]] and let <math>\Delta (\mathcal A)</math> be its [[structure space]] equipped with the [[relative topology|relative]] [[weak topology|weak*-topology]] of the [[continuous dual space|dual]] <math>{\mathcal A}^*</math>. Each element <math>x\in\mathcal A</math> determines its [[Gelfand transform]]
<math display="block">\widehat{x}(\varphi)=\varphi(x), \qquad \varphi\in\Delta(\mathcal A).</math>
A closed subset <math>F\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)</math> is a boundary if
<math display="block">\max_{\varphi\in\Delta(\mathcal A)} |\widehat{x}(\varphi)| = \max_{\varphi\in F} |\widehat{x}(\varphi)|</math>
for every <math>x\in\mathcal A</math>.

The set <math display="inline">S = \bigcap\{F:F \text{ is a boundary of } {\mathcal A}\}</math> is called the '''Shilov boundary'''. It has been proved by Shilov<ref>Theorem 4.15.4 in [[Einar Hille]], [[Ralph S. Phillips]]: [http://www.ams.org/online_bks/coll31/coll31-chIV.pdf Functional analysis and semigroups]. -- AMS, Providence 1957.</ref> that <math>S</math> is a boundary of <math>{\mathcal A}</math>.

Thus one may also say that Shilov boundary is ''the'' minimal boundary of <math>\mathcal A</math>; that is, the unique set <math>S \subset \Delta \mathcal A</math> which satisfies
#<math>S</math> is a boundary of <math>\mathcal A</math>, and
#whenever <math>F</math> is a boundary of <math>\mathcal A</math>, then <math>S \subseteq F</math>.

== Examples ==
If <math>X</math> is a compact Hausdorff space and <math>\mathcal A=C(X)</math>, then the Shilov boundary is all of <math>X</math>.

Let <math>\mathbb D=\{z \in \Complex:|z|<1\}</math> be the [[open unit disc]] in the [[complex plane]] and let <math>A(\mathbb D)</math> denote the [[disc algebra]], consisting of the complex-valued functions continuous on <math>\overline{\mathbb D}</math> and holomorphic on <math>\mathbb D</math>, with [[supremum norm]] and usual algebraic operations. Then <math>\Delta {\mathcal A} = \bar{\mathbb D}</math> and <math>S=\{|z|=1\}</math>.

More generally, the Shilov boundary of a [[polydisc]] <math>\mathbb D_1\times \mathbb D_2\times\cdots\times\mathbb D_k</math> is the product of the boundaries <math>\partial\mathbb D_1\times\partial\mathbb D_2\times\cdots\times\partial\mathbb D_k</math>, and one has the [[Cauchy integral formula]] in the polydisc.

== Bounded symmetric domains ==

In the setting of [[several complex variables]] and [[Hermitian symmetric space]]s, the Shilov boundary admits a particularly concrete geometric description.  Let <math>D</math> be a bounded symmetric domain in its Harish-Chandra realization, and let <math>G=\operatorname{Aut}(D)^\circ</math> be the identity component of its [[biholomorphism]] group.  Then the Shilov boundary <math>S</math> is the smallest closed subset of the topological boundary <math>\partial D</math> on which every function holomorphic on <math>D</math> and continuous on <math>\overline D</math> attains its maximum modulus.<ref name="BIW2007">{{cite journal |last1=Burger |first1=Marc |last2=Iozzi |first2=Alessandra |last3=Wienhard |first3=Anna |title=Hermitian symmetric spaces and Kähler rigidity |journal=Transformation Groups |volume=12 |issue=1 |year=2007 |pages=5–32 |doi=10.1007/s00031-005-1135-0|hdl=20.500.11850/6775 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

For [[bounded symmetric domain]]s this analytic boundary coincides with a distinguished homogeneous boundary orbit: the Shilov boundary is the unique closed <math>G</math>-orbit in <math>\partial D</math>.<ref name="BIW2007" /><ref name="BurgerIozziLabourieWienhard2005">{{cite journal |last1=Burger |first1=Marc |last2=Iozzi |first2=Alessandra |last3=Labourie |first3=François |last4=Wienhard |first4=Anna |title=Maximal Representations of Surface Groups: Symplectic Anosov Structures |journal=Pure and Applied Mathematics Quarterly |volume=1 |issue=3 |year=2005 |pages=555–601}}</ref>  Equivalently, if the domain is irreducible then <math>S</math> is a compact homogeneous space of the form <math>G/Q</math>, where <math>Q</math> is a suitable maximal parabolic subgroup.<ref name="BIW2007" /><ref name="KZ2012">{{cite journal |last1=Koufany |first1=Khalid |last2=Zhang |first2=Genkai |title=Hua operators, Poisson transform and relative discrete series on line bundles over bounded symmetric domains |journal=Journal of Functional Analysis |volume=262 |issue=9 |year=2012 |pages=4140–4159}}</ref>  In real rank one this Shilov boundary is the whole topological boundary, but in higher rank it is usually a proper subset of <math>\partial D</math>.<ref name="BurgerIozziLabourieWienhard2005" />

This description is closely related to the [[Hermitian symmetric space#Borel embedding|Borel embedding]] and to the structure theory of Hermitian symmetric spaces.  In the language of [[Jordan triple system]]s, the Shilov boundary can also be described as the set of maximal tripotents; this point of view is often useful in the study of boundary geometry, transversality, and the [[Cayley transform]].<ref name="Clerc2007">{{cite journal |last=Clerc |first=Jean-Louis |title=An invariant for triples in the Shilov boundary of a bounded symmetric domain |journal=Communications in Analysis and Geometry |volume=15 |issue=1 |year=2007 |pages=147–174 |doi=10.4310/CAG.2007.v15.n1.a5}}</ref><ref name="KZ2012" />

=== Classical examples ===

For the [[Symmetric space|Cartan type I classical domain]]
:<math display="block">\mathcal D_{p,q}=\{Z\in M_{q,p}(\mathbf C): I_p-Z^*Z>0\},</math>
the Shilov boundary is
:<math display="block">S_{p,q}=\{Z\in M_{q,p}(\mathbf C): I_p-Z^*Z=0\}.</math>
Under the Borel embedding, this may be identified with the space of maximal totally isotropic <math>p</math>-planes for the Hermitian form of signature <math>(p,q)</math>; equivalently, it is a homogeneous space for <math>\mathrm{SU}(p,q)</math>.<ref name="BIW2007" />

For the [[Siegel domain|Siegel upper half-space]] (or, equivalently, the bounded symmetric domain associated to <math>\mathrm{Sp}(2n,\mathbf R)</math>), the Shilov boundary can be identified with the [[Lagrangian Grassmannian]], the space of Lagrangian subspaces in a real symplectic vector space.<ref name="BurgerIozziLabourieWienhard2005" />  In the bounded realization by symmetric matrices, it is also described as the compact manifold of unitary symmetric matrices.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Friedland |first=Shmuel |title=Revisiting the Siegel upper half plane I |year=2003 |url=https://www.math.uic.edu/~friedlan/siegelm.pdf}}</ref>

For tube-type bounded symmetric domains, the Shilov boundary has additional structure coming from the corresponding [[Euclidean Jordan algebra]].  This extra structure plays an important role in harmonic analysis on the boundary, in the theory of [[Poisson kernel]], and in the study of invariants such as the [[Maslov index]].<ref name="Clerc2007" /><ref name="KZ2012" />

=== Tube domains and tube type ===

A bounded symmetric domain is said to be '''of tube type''' if it is biholomorphically equivalent to a domain of the form
:<math display="block">T_\Omega = V + i\Omega,</math>
where <math>V</math> is a finite-dimensional real vector space and <math>\Omega \subset V</math> is an open convex cone.<ref name="FK94">{{cite book |last1=Faraut |first1=Jacques |last2=Korányi |first2=Adam |title=Analysis on Symmetric Cones |series=Oxford Mathematical Monographs |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1994}}</ref>  
For irreducible bounded symmetric domains, this is equivalent to the existence of an underlying [[Euclidean Jordan algebra]] structure on <math>V</math>; in that case <math>\Omega</math> is the cone of squares in the Jordan algebra, and the tube domain and its bounded realization are related by a generalized [[Cayley transform]].<ref name="FK94" /><ref name="Clerc2007">{{cite journal |last=Clerc |first=Jean-Louis |title=An invariant for triples in the Shilov boundary of a bounded symmetric domain |journal=Communications in Analysis and Geometry |volume=15 |issue=1 |year=2007 |pages=147–174 |doi=10.4310/CAG.2007.v15.n1.a5}}</ref>

In the tube-type case, the Shilov boundary has an especially explicit description.  If <math>D</math> is realized as the unit ball of the complexification of a Euclidean Jordan algebra <math>V</math>, then the Shilov boundary is the set of maximal tripotents.<ref name="Clerc2007" /><ref name="ClercNeeb2006">{{cite journal |last1=Clerc |first1=Jean-Louis |last2=Neeb |first2=Karl-Hermann |title=Orbits of triples in the Shilov boundary of a bounded symmetric domain |journal=Transformation Groups |volume=11 |issue=3 |year=2006 |pages=387–426 |doi=10.1007/s00031-005-1117-2|arxiv=math/0511259}}</ref>  
Under the unbounded tube realization <math>T_\Omega</math>, the relevant boundary is most naturally described via the compact homogeneous space <math>G/P</math>, in which the real vector space <math>V</math> appears as a dense open affine chart.<ref name="ClercNeeb2006" /><ref name="Zhang1995" /> Equivalently, it is a compact homogeneous space for the automorphism group of the domain.<ref name="Zhang1995">{{cite journal |last=Zhang |first=Genkai |title=Jordan algebras and generalized principal series |journal=Mathematische Annalen |volume=302 |issue=4 |year=1995 |pages=773–786 |doi=10.1007/BF01444516}}</ref><ref name="ClercNeeb2006" /> For symmetric spaces of rank 1, this is the usual (one point) [[conformal compactification]] of <math>V</math>.

Tube type is important because bounded symmetric domains of tube type carry additional boundary geometry not present in general.  In particular, one has a well-developed notion of transversality on the Shilov boundary, and associated invariants such as the [[Maslov index]] play a central role in the geometry of triples of boundary points and in representation theory.<ref name="Clerc2007" /><ref name="ClercNeeb2006" />  This extra structure is also fundamental in harmonic analysis on the boundary, including Poisson transforms and Hardy-type spaces.<ref name="Zhang1995" />

An example is the [[Siegel upper half-space]]
:<math display="block">\mathfrak H_n = \{ Z \in \operatorname{Sym}_n(\mathbf C) : \operatorname{Im} Z > 0\},</math>
which is a tube domain over the cone of real positive-definite symmetric matrices.  Its bounded realization is the symplectic bounded symmetric domain, and its Shilov boundary can be identified with the [[Lagrangian Grassmannian]].<ref name="BurgerIozziLabourieWienhard2005">{{cite journal |last1=Burger |first1=Marc |last2=Iozzi |first2=Alessandra |last3=Labourie |first3=François |last4=Wienhard |first4=Anna |title=Maximal Representations of Surface Groups: Symplectic Anosov Structures |journal=Pure and Applied Mathematics Quarterly |volume=1 |issue=3 |year=2005 |pages=555–601}}</ref>

== Uniform algebras ==

The Shilov boundary of a [[uniform algebra]]s often admits a more explicit description.  Let <math>X</math> be a compact Hausdorff space, and let <math>A\subseteq C(X)</math> be a unital subalgebra that is closed in the [[supremum norm]] and separates points of <math>X</math>.  Such an algebra is called a uniform algebra.  A closed subset <math>F\subseteq X</math> is called a boundary for <math>A</math> if every function <math>f\in A</math> attains its maximum modulus on <math>F</math>, that is,
:<math display="block">\|f\|_\infty=\max_{x\in F}|f(x)|</math>
for all <math>f\in A</math>.  The Shilov boundary of <math>A</math> is the smallest closed boundary in this sense.

For a uniform algebra, the maximal ideal space of <math>A</math> can be identified with a compact space containing a copy of <math>X</math>. In many classical examples the Shilov boundary may be viewed directly as a distinguished closed subset of <math>X</math> itself.  For example, if <math>A=C(X)</math>, then every point of <math>X</math> is needed, so the Shilov boundary is all of <math>X</math>.  For the [[disc algebra]] <math>A(\mathbb D)</math>, the Shilov boundary is the unit circle <math>\partial\mathbb D</math>.

For product uniform algebras, the Shilov boundary is the product of the Shilov boundaries of the factors.  In particular, the Shilov boundary of the polydisc algebra <math>A(\mathbb D^n)</math> is the torus <math>\mathbb T^n</math>, as noted earlier.

The Shilov boundary is closely related to the theory of ''peak points''.  A point <math>x\in X</math> is called a peak point for <math>A</math> if there exists a function <math>f\in A</math> such that <math>f(x)=1</math> and <math>|f(y)|<1</math> for all <math>y\neq x</math>.  Every peak point belongs to the Shilov boundary.  In many classical uniform algebras, the closure of the set of peak points coincides with the Shilov boundary.

From this point of view, the Shilov boundary is the smallest closed subset of the underlying compact space that still determines the supremum norm of every function in the algebra.  This makes it a natural analogue, for function algebras, of the topological boundary in the [[maximum modulus principle]] for holomorphic functions.
